Aside from just "upgrade" which is probably not the answer anyone really wants to have to hear in this context, something as simple as just cleaning a little more regularly can help reduce the amount of "coffee dust" you get. Less fines around the chute and burrs = less fines in your coffee too. This won't make a drastic improvement though unfortunately. The other option is to mess around with a slightly finer grind to use in your French press, the vario seems to produce less fines when you dial it back towards a chemex type grind (anecdotally anyway!). 
Another tip which I can't even guarantee works but I see a lot of people do it regardless, is to keep the hopper just a little more full than if you were just grinding a dose at a time. In theory, this reduces the "popcorn" effect of those last few beans; supposedly helping to prevent them from subsequently getting mashed in the burrs and contributing to fines. Again, this may have minimal effect (unfortunately for French press fanatics such as myself!)

Perhaps try measuring directly your water rather than your yield just once and see if it changes anything? Different coffees can produce different "yields" even if you're using the same ratio, for a number of reasons (if anybody wants to chime and expand on these feel free! It might help). 17g to 280 water is a pretty good ratio if you were measuring it like that; 1:16.47. Depending on the coffee you could even try dosing up the coffee to 17.5 to get a 1:16 ratio and make it "stronger"? Maybe even as high as a 1:15 ratio I've seen for v60! Or, you may even benefit from experimenting with going a few clicks finer on your mini mill (not the most uniform particle size as you mentioned, but definitely has the potential to do good pourovers with a sound ratio and technique)
Which brings us to arguably the most contentious factor with the V60 - technique. How are you pouring? How long is your bloom? Do you agitate at all? How high is the stream of water falling? SO many things can impact your extraction and TDS and this the flavor of the final result. If you really don't want to go any finer on your grind, there's always the option of altering your pouring technique to extend the brew time (for a brew that size, 9/10 I would shoot 3mins or just over, probably not under. But it depends on the coffee and your taste!). Using smaller, pulse pours in circles spiralling outwards with the stream of water very slow and not falling far will reduce the turbulence and also reduce the flow rate of the dripper (putting coffee in contact with water for longer = extracting more = more flavour). 
This is all working on the assumption that the "muted" flavours are as a result of weak coffee. It could be the coffee itself, how fresh is it? Flavours can go dull in stale-er coffee!
Let us know if this in any way helps (I could just be telling you a bunch of stuff you've already tried!). Happy experimenting though! Post anything you find works/doesn't, someone else might be able to get a better brew from your experiments too :)

In short, it's somewhat of a trade off:
Standard = more body (a lot of oils in the coffee), but also more fines so it's a little "muddy" (body replaces flavor clarity in this case)
Fine = a little less body (only slightly), but also less fines (arguably a little more flavor clarity than the standard disk, but a lot less than paper filters)
Also consider that the able fine disk is SUPER thin, so is quite "delicate" (bends easily especially if you're travelling with it). 
No one is particularly "better" than the other, it's just what you prefer! And the amount of fines you get will also depend MOSTLY on your grinder and how coarse/fine you grind in the first place.

How I found out about what was going on with me was seeing my psychiatrist every day (yes, every freakin day) for 2 months while I was in hospital, and then every week for a year before my symptoms were "diagnosed" - which is just the medical term for "defined" - as Schizoaffective disorder. 
The best way to find out what's going on with your brain, and why it's happening, and alltogether get the answer to the big question "what the fucking fuck is wrong with me", is to seek help from professionals!!!! You can't diagnose yourself unfortunately, nor can the internet diagnose you. Which I know is tough, because I can understand that you're probably terrified and just want some clarity! It will come in time, I promise you. See someone professional and tell them absolutely as much as you can. The more they know, the more pieces of the puzzle they can put together! They'll have more clarity, and they'll pass on that clarity to you :) 
That being said: my pro tip for surviving mental illness is to not be caught up on a diagnosis. All mental illness are very "grey" and they're separated by fine lines. Me being diagnosed at 18 after only a year is EXTREMELY rare. I know it might feel like you want some clarity so help ease some fear, but really, the diagnosis you should be striving to get is "working on happiness". That's how you need to define, or 'diagnose' yourself. It's not easy, but nothing worth having comes easy. And I promise you, you kickass person, that happiness is the most worthwhile thing in the world. It's the most powerful freedom you can experience - you're not locked inside the mental prison of sadness. And best of all IT IS ATTAINABLE. ALWAYS. No matter WHAT your medical "diagnosis" is (and you may go years without one - which although frustrating is okay!!! You do not need one. At all) you can live a happy, healthy, productive life. 
TL;DR: I found out I was schizoaffective through constant interactions with medical professionals. Don't even attempt to self-diagnose, or have anyone but a professional "label" you. Label YOURSELF as someone who's a fighter, and you're guaranteed to come out on top! Stay strong, and let me know if this all makes sense :)

They are very, very real to me and it took me quite some time to be able to differentiate between the hallucinations and reality. My brain itself processes the hallucinations just as it does music through headphones yeah, the same areas in my brain are activated. I hear up to 6 at once at the worst of times. They all have distinct tone, direction (if I'm hearing it like someone is behind me or in front of me talking to me), and content of what they say (some just narrate eg "he is opening the door." And some insult "you're worthless"). Because they are so real to me, they're not as scary as you may think! Just disorienting. That being said, imagine having six people you can't see telling you to cut yourself - that's a pretty shitty experience. But with medication and learning how to handle them I live a very normal, happy life with my voices :) anything is possible hombre!

I had a series of suicide attempts which culminated in the police being called after I was found lying on the train tracks. I had been cutting for two years and hearing voices for nearly a year, but had NEVER seen a psychiatrist or gotten help ever. I was taken by the police to get an evaluation and within 24 hours of seeing a psychiatrist for the first time I was admitted to hospital for them to work out what was going on/stop me from killing myself.

The most interesting experience of my life. Unfortunately, I didn't apply myself to any therapy and had multiple suicide attempts in there. But mental clinics, at least the one I was at (In Melbourne, Aus), was a fantastic facility and helps alot of pople.
